comparison.summary: Four JavaScript approaches are available here. The new binary-search and rolling-hash solution verifies actual elements, fixing the collision issue in the older hash-only Python approach; the three existing suffix solutions remain unchanged.
details: The new rolling-hash version binary-searches the length and groups windows by hash, then compares their actual elements before combining occurrence counts. It takes O(n log n + C) time with expected constant-time Map operations, where C counts all exact element comparisons, and O(n) space. A conservative worst-case time bound is O(n³ log n).
The simple suffix version copies and sorts whole suffixes, then compares neighboring suffixes directly. It is exact, but takes O(n² log n) time with O(n log n) sort comparisons and O(n²) space.

The optimized suffix array version uses rank doubling and stable counting sort, then Kasai’s algorithm for adjacent LCP values. It applies the same unique-prefix formula in O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
The suffix automaton propagates occurrence counts through the shorterId tree and finds the shortest length represented by a node that occurs once. It takes O(n) expected time and O(n) space.

The older Python solution binary-searches the length and counts rolling hashes without checking the actual elements, taking O(n log n) time and O(n) space. That hash-only comparison is incorrect for nums = [1,20,2,1,20,2]: it returns 3 instead of 2. With base 19, [1,20] and [2,1] both hash to 39, hiding the unique pair [2,1]. All four saved JavaScript solutions return the correct answer 2.

Choosing a base larger than the values prevents that base-19 example from colliding, but modular collisions can still happen. The new solution handles those too by keeping separate exact-window groups under the same hash.

solutions.title: Binary search + rolling hash
solutions.approach: Binary-search the smallest length for which some continuous subarray occurs exactly once. For each tested length, build the first window’s polynomial hash, then slide by removing the outgoing value’s weighted contribution, shifting the remaining weights, and adding the incoming value. Store a list of representative windows and occurrence counts under each hash. When hashes match, compare the actual elements before increasing a count; different sequences keep separate groups. After recording every window, a group with count 1 means this length works, so search shorter lengths. Otherwise, search longer lengths. A unique window can always be extended while remaining unique, which makes binary search valid.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n log n + C) with expected constant-time Map operations; O(n³ log n) conservative worst case

variables.C: Total element comparisons in sameWindow across all tested lengths, including comparisons between matching duplicate windows and between different windows that share a hash.

notes: Equal hashes are only a reason to compare two windows, not proof that they are equal. Exact element checks keep this version correct even when different windows share a hash.
Large inputs with many repeated windows can make exact comparisons expensive. The optimized suffix array and suffix automaton solutions below offer stronger performance bounds.
solutions.walkthroughMarkdown:
#### 1. Input and the question we are answering

Use `nums = [1, 2, 1, 2, 1]`. A subarray is a continuous part of this array. We want the shortest length whose subarray appears **exactly once**. Overlapping occurrences count separately.

| Index | Value |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1 |
| 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 1 |
| 3 | 2 |
| 4 | 1 |

A window is one subarray of the length currently being tested. `start` is its first index. `hasUnique(length)` returns whether **any** window of that length occurs once; it does not require every window to be unique.

#### 2. Scan the values and choose the base

Set `n = nums.length = 5` and `largest = 0`. The `for...of` loop visits every value in order:

| Index visited | Update to `largest` |
|---:|---|
| `0` | `Math.max(0, 1) = 1` |
| `1` | `Math.max(1, 2) = 2` |
| `2` | `Math.max(2, 1) = 2` |
| `3` | `Math.max(2, 2) = 2` |
| `4` | `Math.max(2, 1) = 2` |

All five values have been visited, so the loop ends. Set `BASE = largest + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3` and `MOD = 1000000007`.

Multiplying by `BASE` shifts the existing values one position to the left in the hash. For `[a, b, c]`, the hash before taking the remainder is `a × BASE² + b × BASE + c`. With `BASE = 3`, the weights are `9, 3, 1`: `[1, 2, 1]` becomes `1 × 9 + 2 × 3 + 1 = 16`. The `% MOD` operation keeps the remainder after division by `1000000007`, so the stored hash stays bounded.

The base is larger than every input value, but taking a remainder can still make different windows have the same hash. The code checks their actual elements before treating them as the same window.

#### 3. Why we can binary-search the length

If a unique window has length less than `n`, extend it by one element. Extend to the right when a following element exists; if the window ends at the last index, extend to the left. Because the window is shorter than `n`, an element exists to its left in that case. If that longer window occurred twice, the original window would also occur twice at the same position inside those two occurrences. That contradicts the original window being unique. Therefore, once a length works, every larger length works.

A successful check lets us search shorter lengths. A failed check lets us search longer lengths. The whole array occurs once, so length `n` is always a valid initial answer.

Set `lo = 1`, `hi = n = 5`, and `answer = n = 5`. No calls to `hasUnique` have happened yet.

In the snapshots below, `16 → [{ start: 0, count: 2 }]` means: hash `16` has a list containing one group; its representative window starts at index `0`, and that exact sequence has appeared twice. The code stores starting indices and counts, not copies of the windows. A list can contain multiple groups if different sequences share one hash.

#### 4. Binary-search check 1: length 3

`lo <= hi` is `1 <= 5`, which is true. Calculate `mid = Math.floor((1 + 5) / 2) = Math.floor(3) = 3`. Call `hasUnique(3)`.

**Calculate the first value’s weight.**

Set `highestPower = 1`. Start the power loop with `i = 1`.

- `i = 1`: `1 < 3` is true. Set `highestPower = (1 × 3) % 1000000007 = 3 % 1000000007 = 3`. Increase `i` to `2`.

- `i = 2`: `2 < 3` is true. Set `highestPower = (3 × 3) % 1000000007 = 9 % 1000000007 = 9`. Increase `i` to `3`.

- `i = 3`: `3 < 3` is false. Stop the power loop. The first value’s weight is `BASE^(3 - 1)`, stored modulo `MOD` as `9`.

**Start this check with fresh state.** Create a new empty `groupsByHash` Map and set `hash = 0`. Counts from another length are not reused.

```text
(empty Map)
```

**Build the first window: indices `0` through `2`, values `[1, 2, 1]`.**

- `i = 0`: `0 < 3` is true. Read `nums[0] = 1`. Set `hash = (0 × 3 + 1) % 1000000007 = 1 % 1000000007 = 1`. Increase `i` to `1`.

- `i = 1`: `1 < 3` is true. Read `nums[1] = 2`. Set `hash = (1 × 3 + 2) % 1000000007 = 5 % 1000000007 = 5`. Increase `i` to `2`.

- `i = 2`: `2 < 3` is true. Read `nums[2] = 1`. Set `hash = (5 × 3 + 1) % 1000000007 = 16 % 1000000007 = 16`. Increase `i` to `3`.

- `i = 3`: `3 < 3` is false. Stop building the initial hash.

**Record start `0`, window `[1, 2, 1]`, hash `16`.**

`groupsByHash.get(16)` returns `undefined`, so `!groups` is true. Create `groups = []` and call `groupsByHash.set(16, groups)`. This new bucket is now `16 → []`.

The group loop visits no groups because the list is empty.

Push `{ start: 0, count: 1 }` into the list. This is the first occurrence of this exact window. Reach the end of `recordWindow` and return to `hasUnique`.

**Slide to start `1`.** The loop condition is `1 + 3 <= 5`, or `4 <= 5`, which is true. The new window is `[2, 1, 2]` at indices `1` through `3`.

3. Read the incoming value, `nums[1 + 3 - 1] = nums[3] = 2`. Shift the remaining weights and append it: `hash = (7 × 3 + 2) % 1000000007 = 23 % 1000000007 = 23`.

3. Read the incoming value, `nums[3 + 2 - 1] = nums[4] = 1`. Shift the remaining weights and append it: `hash = (2 × 3 + 1) % 1000000007 = 7 % 1000000007 = 7`.

**Record start `3`, window `[2, 1]`, hash `7`.**

Map before recording:

```text
5 → [{ start: 0, count: 2 }]
7 → [{ start: 1, count: 1 }]
```

`groupsByHash.get(7)` returns `[{ start: 1, count: 1 }]`, so `!groups` is false. Keep this existing list.

Visit group `{ start: 1, count: 1 }` and call `sameWindow(1, 3)`:

- `offset = 0`: `0 < 2` is true. Compare `nums[1 + 0] = nums[1] = 2` with `nums[3 + 0] = nums[3] = 2`. They are equal, so the mismatch condition is false. Increase `offset` to `1`.

- `offset = 1`: `1 < 2` is true. Compare `nums[1 + 1] = nums[2] = 1` with `nums[3 + 1] = nums[4] = 1`. They are equal, so the mismatch condition is false. Increase `offset` to `2`.

- `offset = 2`: `2 < 2` is false. End the comparison loop and return `true` from `sameWindow`.

Because the windows match, increase this group’s `count` from `1` to `2`. `recordWindow` returns immediately. It does not push a new group or visit another group.

Map after recording:

```text
5 → [{ start: 0, count: 2 }]
7 → [{ start: 1, count: 2 }]
```

Increase `start` from `3` to `4`.

At `start = 4`, the slide-loop condition is `4 + 2 <= 5`, or `6 <= 5`, which is false. Every length-2 window has now been recorded.

**Scan the completed counts in Map insertion order.** We wait until all windows are recorded: a window seen once early in the scan could appear again later.

Visit the list for hash `5`: `[{ start: 0, count: 2 }]`.

- Visit `{ start: 0, count: 2 }`, representing `[1, 2]`. Check `group.count === 1`: `2 === 1` is `false`.

- Do not return. This bucket has no more groups, so continue to the next bucket.

Visit the list for hash `7`: `[{ start: 1, count: 2 }]`.

- Visit `{ start: 1, count: 2 }`, representing `[2, 1]`. Check `group.count === 1`: `2 === 1` is `false`.

- Do not return. This bucket has no more groups, so continue to the next bucket.

No buckets remain. Both count loops finish without finding a count of `1`. Reach `return false`, so `hasUnique(2)` returns `false`.

**Update the search.** `hasUnique(2)` is false, so set `lo = mid + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3` (`2 → 3`). `hi` stays `2` and `answer` stays `3`. The search state is now `lo = 3`, `hi = 2`, `answer = 3`.

#### 7. Finish the search

Check `lo <= hi` again: `3 <= 2` is false. Exit the `while` loop and execute `return answer`, which returns `3`.

Every tested length has been fully checked:

| Length | Result | Reason |
|---:|---|---|
| 3 | `true` | `[2, 1, 2]` occurs once, at start `1`. |
| 1 | `false` | `[1]` occurs three times; `[2]` occurs twice. |
| 2 | `false` | `[1, 2]` and `[2, 1]` each occur twice. |

The shortest unique subarray is `[2, 1, 2]`, so its length is **3**. Binary search did not call `hasUnique(4)` or `hasUnique(5)`; the trace above includes every call it actually made.

#### 8. A collision example: one length-2 check

This is a separate, focused illustration of hash collisions at **fixed length 2**, not a second binary-search trace. Use `nums = [1, 9994, 100000, 10001, 1, 9994, 100000, 10001]`. Its maximum value is `100000`, so `BASE = 100000 + 1 = 100001`; `MOD` remains `1000000007`.

For two values, the polynomial is `first × BASE + second`:

- `[1, 9994]`: `1 × 100001 + 9994 = 109995`; `109995 % 1000000007 = 109995`.

- `[10001, 1]`: `10001 × 100001 + 1 = 1000110002`; `1000110002 % 1000000007 = 109995`.

The raw values differ by exactly `1000110002 - 109995 = 1000000007`, so the remainder is the same even though the arrays are different.

All seven length-2 windows have these hashes:

| Start | Window | Hash |
|---:|---|---:|
| `0` | `[1, 9994]` | `109995` |
| `1` | `[9994, 100000]` | `999509994` |
| `2` | `[100000, 10001]` | `109931` |
| `3` | `[10001, 1]` | `109995` |
| `4` | `[1, 9994]` | `109995` |
| `5` | `[9994, 100000]` | `999509994` |
| `6` | `[100000, 10001]` | `109931` |

Follow the bucket for hash `109995`:

1. At start `0`, no bucket exists. Create an empty list and push `{ start: 0, count: 1 }` for `[1, 9994]`. The bucket becomes `109995 → [{ start: 0, count: 1 }]`.

2. Starts `1` and `2` use other hash buckets, so this bucket stays `109995 → [{ start: 0, count: 1 }]`.

3. At start `3`, the hash is also `109995`. Before recording, the bucket is `109995 → [{ start: 0, count: 1 }]`. Visit its group and call `sameWindow(0, 3)`. At `offset = 0`, `0 < 2` is true. Compare `nums[0 + 0] = 1` with `nums[3 + 0] = 10001`. They differ, so return `false` immediately; offset `1` is not visited. The existing group’s count stays `1`. No more groups exist, so push `{ start: 3, count: 1 }`. The bucket becomes `109995 → [{ start: 0, count: 1 }, { start: 3, count: 1 }]`.

4. At start `4`, the hash is `109995` again. Before recording, the bucket is `109995 → [{ start: 0, count: 1 }, { start: 3, count: 1 }]`. Visit the first group and call `sameWindow(0, 4)`. At offset `0`, `0 < 2` is true and `nums[0] = 1` equals `nums[4] = 1`; advance to offset `1`. At offset `1`, `1 < 2` is true and `nums[1] = 9994` equals `nums[5] = 9994`; advance to offset `2`. Now `2 < 2` is false, so return `true`. Increase the first group’s count `1 → 2` and return from `recordWindow`; the second group is not compared. The bucket becomes `109995 → [{ start: 0, count: 2 }, { start: 3, count: 1 }]`.

5. Starts `5` and `6` use other hash buckets. The final collision bucket remains `109995 → [{ start: 0, count: 2 }, { start: 3, count: 1 }]`. The other two buckets each contain one group with count `2`.

6. The final count scan visits hash `109995` first. Its start-`0` group has count `2`, so it continues. Its start-`3` group has count `1`, so `hasUnique(2)` returns `true` immediately; the other buckets are not visited. `[10001, 1]` is unique.

Every individual value in this example occurs twice, so length `1` fails and the correct shortest length is `2`. Counting only hashes would merge the two different groups into one count of `3`, miss this unique pair, and incorrectly return `3` for the problem. Comparing the actual elements keeps the answer exact.

#### 9. Time, space, and what the extra comparisons cost

Let `n` be the number of elements and `C` be the total number of element comparisons performed by `sameWindow` across **all tested lengths**. `C` includes comparisons between truly identical windows as well as comparisons caused by accidental hash collisions. The main example performs `3 + 3 + 4 = 10` such comparisons.

The maximum scan costs `O(n)`. Hash construction, sliding, and creating or updating at most one group per window cost `O(n)` per check, assuming expected constant-time Map operations. Every candidate group visited during the bucket search performs at least one element comparison, so that search overhead is covered by `C`. Binary search tests `O(log n)` lengths, so total time is **`O(n log n + C)`**. A conservative worst-case bound is **`O(n³ log n)`**: a check can compare `O(n²)` pairs of windows and inspect up to `O(n)` elements per pair.

Space is **`O(n)`**: one check stores at most one group per window, using a start index and a count. It does not copy subarrays. The next check creates a fresh Map, and the old one is no longer needed.

Exact comparisons can be expensive on large inputs with many repeated windows. The optimized suffix array and suffix automaton solutions below avoid this repeated element-by-element verification.

solutions.title: Simple suffix sorting + LCP
solutions.approach: Copy every suffix and sort those arrays lexicographically. For each suffix, compare its elements with the previous and next suffix to find their longest common prefixes (LCP). A unique prefix needs max(previous LCP, next LCP) + 1 elements; take the smallest such length that fits inside its suffix.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n² log n) with O(n log n) sort comparisons
notes: This version makes the steps easier to follow, but copies n(n + 1) / 2 elements. Use an optimized version for large inputs such as 100,000 numbers.

solutions.title: Optimized suffix array + LCP
solutions.approach: Sort suffix starting indices without copying the suffixes: rank doubling compares increasingly long prefixes using stable counting sorts. Kasai’s algorithm calculates neighboring LCP values while reusing matches from the previous suffix. For each suffix, compute max(previous LCP, next LCP) + 1 and take the smallest length that fits inside that suffix.
notes: This optimized version uses the separate function name smallestUniqueSubarraySuffixArray.

solutions.title: Suffix automaton
solutions.approach: Build a suffix automaton that groups subarrays sharing the same ending positions. Add each node’s occurrence count to its shorterId parent after processing its children. For a node seen exactly once, nodes[shorterId].maxLength + 1 is its shortest unique length; take the minimum of those lengths.
notes: Preserved naming: currNum, newId, lastId, shorterId, nextId, cloneId, ROOT_ID, and NO_ID. Transitions remain plain JavaScript objects.
